headline: Trump adds Iran 'better negotiate a fair deal'
dek: Trump followed his 'considering limited strikes' remark by telling reporters Iran 'better negotiate a fair deal.' Rezazadeh: both sides have presented sets of conditions through the mediators (Qatar and Oman); Iran awaiting US acceptance of its conditions; contacts overseen by Iran's Supreme…
sources: Donald Trump (remarks to reporters, Friday); Yaqoub Rezazadeh, Iranian parliament Nat'l Security and Foreign Policy Committee (via ILNA)
fault_line: Are these real negotiations, or Trump performing 'dealmaker' pressure while keeping the strike option loaded?

sections.what_happened: Donald Trump has added a new condition to the standoff, telling reporters that Iran 'better negotiate a fair deal,' days after saying he was considering limited strikes. On the Iranian side, parliament National Security Committee member Yaqoub Rezazadeh told the ILNA news agency that both sides have exchanged sets of conditions through the Qatari and Omani mediators, that Iran is awaiting Washington's acceptance of its conditions, and that the contacts are overseen by Iran's Supreme National Security Council.
sections.what_verified: Trump's remarks are widely reported. Rezazadeh's account — conditions exchanged via Qatar and Oman, Supreme National Security Council oversight — is carried in the Dawn live blog quoting ILNA. It is consistent with Foreign Minister Araghchi's statement to MSNOW that a draft deal could reach envoy Witkoff within two to three days, and with the White House's own 'positive and constructive' framing of the channel. The mediator pair — Qatar and Oman — matches the established back-channel architecture.
sections.what_disputed: The contents of the conditions on either side have no independent confirmation — both capitals describe the other's homework without showing it. Trump's claim that Iran is 'losing so badly' sits awkwardly next to his own earlier rejection of the UNGA-week proposal as 'unacceptable': if Tehran is collapsing, the deal should have been easy in September. Which Trump is negotiating — the one who says Iran is finished, or the one demanding a 'fair deal' — is genuinely unclear, and that ambiguity is the story.
sections.why_matters: The talks are real, but the leverage is not diplomacy — it is the strait. Iran negotiates as the country that can close the world's most important waterway, with the IRGC's seizure campaign and the Ansar Allah pressure campaign both demonstrating the cost of escalation in real time. Trump's 'better negotiate' is pressure; Rezazadeh's 'we await your acceptance' is the counter. The side that needs the deal less sets the terms, and right now neither side is sure which one that is.
sections.context: Oman and Qatar have run the United States-Iran back channel for years — Muscat hosted the indirect rounds, Doha the money. The Supreme National Security Council's oversight means this is not freelance diplomacy; it is state policy at the highest level in Tehran. The channel survived the February war and the eight months since, which tells you both sides consider it load-bearing. Trump's public 'limited strikes' musing and the 'fair deal' demand are the pressure track running alongside the quiet track — the classic two-level game.

totw_analysis: Strip away the theatre and this is a leverage negotiation wearing a diplomacy costume. Trump performs the dealmaker — 'better negotiate a fair deal' — while keeping the strike option visibly loaded, because the performance is the pressure. Tehran's answer, delivered through a parliamentarian rather than the foreign ministry, is equally performed: we have tabled our conditions, the ball is in your court, and by the way the Supreme National Security Council is watching. Both sides are negotiating in public for audiences at home while the real exchange happens through Muscat and Doha. Now read it from Tehran's side, because that is where the Western coverage will not go. Iran's leverage is not a talking point; it is two waterways. The Strait of Hormuz, where the IRGC is seizing ships weekly, and the Bab el-Mandeb, where Ansar Allah sets the terms. Every 'better negotiate' from Trump lands in a week when twelve ships have been hit and two container vessels seized. That is not the backdrop to the negotiation. That IS the negotiation. The honest uncertainty: whether Trump's strike talk is a bluff to force the 'fair deal' or the prelude to the 'limited strikes' he keeps mentioning. Tehran is pricing both. The 'fair deal' will be whatever the strait makes necessary.
